clue.text: Extremely boring oldster is young after treatment

indicators.note: Treatment is what is done to something being worked on, and a word worked over comes back with its letters in a fresh arrangement.

parts.note: the fourteen letters of these three words, resettled

explanation.walkthrough: Fourteen letters of fodder for a fourteen-letter answer, which is a useful way to place a long anagram: the definition can only be the two words left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremely boring → SOUL-DESTROYING: work called that is so dull it wears the spirit down, an idiom pitched far stronger than merely tedious.

clue.text: Anticlimactic account of oversexed pet?

parts.note: shaggy leans on the British slang sense of shag, and the question mark flags the liberty
a dog is the household pet the surface has in mind
an account of events is a story, and this word is doing two jobs at once

explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' pulls double duty: it closes the definition and it hands over the last word of the answer. Setters allow themselves that when the surface is this smooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Anticlimactic account → SHAGGY DOG STORY: the name for a long rambling joke whose punchline deliberately fizzles, so the tale is all build-up and no payoff.

clue.text: What to wear in college class

parts.note: uni is the everyday short form of university
a form is a class in a British school

explanation.walkthrough: Two words for places of education sit side by side and neither is the definition. FORM for a school class is the piece worth remembering; it turns up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: What to wear → UNIFORM: a uniform is the outfit a school or a force prescribes, so it is what you are told to wear rather than what you choose.

clue.text: Cabin shutter so easy to pick up?

parts.note: dead works as a flat intensifier the way so does — dead easy, dead right, dead certain
anything light is easy to lift, so the phrase describes the word by what it feels like in the hand

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves lean on loose everyday English rather than abbreviation, which makes them hard to spot. The nautical sense of the definition is the thing to look up and keep.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabin shutter → DEADLIGHT: a deadlight is the hinged steel cover a ship carries over a porthole, closed to keep heavy seas out of the cabin.

clue.text: What you are doing is very caring, nothing omitted

indicators.note: To omit something is to leave it out, so whatever is named beside the word never reaches the answer.

parts.note: so is a plain intensifier, handed over whole
a nought is written O, and this is the letter that gets taken out
LOVING is caring; lose that O and five letters remain

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is pointed straight at the reader, mid-puzzle, which is why it looks like part of the sentence rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: What you are doing → SOLVING: the clue points at the reader in the act of working a crossword, and solving is the verb for exactly that activity.

clue.text: Sink back asleep, shattered after run

indicators.note: Something shattered lies in pieces, and the pieces of a word are letters that have to be picked up in a new order.

parts.note: R is the cricket scoreboard's abbreviation for run
the six letters of asleep, resettled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink back' is the definition and looks like part of the drowsy picture, which is the trap. The R hides in a single word doing service as a cricket score.
explanation.definitionFit: Sink back → RELAPSE: to relapse is to slide back into an illness or a bad habit after a spell of improvement, so the movement is downhill again.

clue.text: The old folks land

indicators.note: Old marks the word beside it as archaic, asking for the antique spelling rather than the modern one.

parts.note: YE is the antique spelling of the, as in ye olde shoppe
folks are people, and men will stand for them here

explanation.walkthrough: The YE spelling comes from a misread Old English letter, the thorn, which printers set as a Y. Setters flag it with 'old', 'once' or 'formerly'.
explanation.definitionFit: land → YEMEN: a country is a land, and this one sits at the southern corner of the Arabian peninsula, so the clue wants an instance of the class.

clue.text: Inquisitively touring island, while playing loud music?

indicators.note: A tour goes right round its destination, so the touring word travels around whatever it visits.

parts.note: to be nosy is to be inquisitive, and the adverb follows
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosy' and 'noisy' are one letter and one idea apart, which is the whole trick — the clue wants you to reach for the inquisitive word first.
explanation.definitionFit: while playing loud music? → NOISILY: noisily is the adverb for doing a thing with plenty of racket, and blasting a stereo is one everyday instance.

clue.text: Grim from the start, hearing cantor messing up old music

indicators.note: To mess something up is to disturb its arrangement, and a disturbed word will not keep its letters in place.
From the start points at where a word begins, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: the first letter of Grim
thirteen letters resettled behind that G

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a cantor being scolded at rehearsal. 'Hearing' is only more material to shuffle, despite looking every inch like an instruction of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: old music → GREGORIAN CHANT: the plainsong of the medieval Western church, sung in unison and named for Pope Gregory, so 'old' does real work.

clue.text: Woman needs a large beer delivered

parts.note: the article taken straight off the page
big is the plain synonym for large

indicators.note: A speech is delivered, so the word beside it is to be spoken rather than spelt.

parts.note: the beer is ALE, and said aloud it can just as well be spelt the other way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' is the giveaway that something here is meant for the ear. Once the beer has been heard, the woman's name is ordinary vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: Woman → ABIGAIL: Abigail is a given name, so the clue names a class and wants one instance — and in old comedy an abigail was a lady's maid.

clue.text: Less smooth piece of sugar? That is right

parts.note: a lump of sugar is the cube that goes in your tea
i.e. is the Latin id est, which translates as that is
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: IE for 'that is' is one of the abbreviations worth owning outright — it appears in hundreds of grids. The sugar lump keeps the surface at the tea table.
explanation.definitionFit: Less smooth → LUMPIER: gravy or a mattress with lumps in it has an uneven surface, so the comparative form is the natural opposite of smoother.

clue.text: Warning sound from half grey bird

indicators.note: Half of a four-letter word is two letters, and the front half is the one meant unless the clue says otherwise.

parts.note: the first half of GREy
an owl is the bird

explanation.walkthrough: OWL is the crossword's default bird — short, vowel-rich, endlessly useful — so it is worth trying whenever a bare 'bird' turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: Warning sound → GROWL: a dog's low rumble is the noise it makes before it bites, so the word names a warning by the animal that gives it.

clue.text: Threatening little devil with termination

parts.note: an imp is the small mischievous devil of folklore
a termination is an ending

explanation.walkthrough: IMP is the crossword's standard little devil. The surface reads as a threat of dismissal, which is exactly the misdirection 'termination' is there to supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Threatening → IMPENDING: something impending is looming over you and about to arrive, which is what we mean by calling a disaster threatening.

clue.text: Democrat, very eager, occasionally pure rabble-rouser

parts.note: Dem is the newspaper shorthand for a Democrat
agog means eagerly expectant

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens at intervals rather than every time, so letters are taken at every other position.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of pUrE

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a party colleague being praised; the definition is the sting waiting in the last word. American politics supplies the opening three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: rabble-rouser → DEMAGOGUE: a demagogue whips up a crowd by playing to its fears rather than arguing, which is exactly what rousing a rabble means.

clue.text: PM, or less important office

parts.note: Theresa May was Prime Minister, and PMs' surnames are standard fodder
the little conjunction is taken at face value, two letters straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: Prime ministers' surnames are a standing resource for setters — May, Heath, Brown, Blair — and here one of them is bolted to the word that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: less important office → MAYOR: a mayor heads a town council, a genuine public post but well below the Prime Minister.

clue.text: Stole time for fixing Christmas decoration

indicators.note: Fixing something means putting its parts back together, and parts of a word put back together need not go back where they were.

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words, resettled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole time' reads as theft and is really a bag of letters, which is the whole deception. The definition sits at the far end, plain as anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas decoration → MISTLETOE: sprigs of the parasitic plant are hung indoors in December, and the kissing custom is why it counts as decoration.

clue.text: Tennis champion finally quit hard work

parts.note: Steffi Graf won twenty-two grand slam singles titles

indicators.note: Finally means at the very end, so it points at the closing letter of the word beside it rather than the word itself.

parts.note: the last letter of quiT

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be about a player retiring. Sporting surnames of exactly four letters — Graf, Borg, Hunt, Owen — are a setter's staple.
explanation.definitionFit: hard work → GRAFT: graft is British slang for sustained toil — 'hard graft' — a sense quite separate from the surgical and horticultural ones.

clue.text: Declare period of history unexceptional

parts.note: to aver is to declare something as fact
an age is a stretch of history, as in the Bronze Age

explanation.walkthrough: AVER is a courtroom verb that earns its keep in grids because of its vowels. The surface plays as a historian being dismissive about a whole century.
explanation.definitionFit: unexceptional → AVERAGE: average means middling, neither good nor bad, so a thing described that way stands out in no direction at all.

clue.text: US state's old university is covered in creeper

indicators.note: To be covered in something is to have it lying over you, so the creeper closes around what it covers.

parts.note: a liana is the woody creeper that climbs rainforest trees
O is the standard abbreviation for old
U is the standard abbreviation for university
the little verb is taken at face value, two letters straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'is' is not holding the sentence together — it is two letters of the answer, and spotting that is the hardest step in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: US state → LOUISIANA: Louisiana is one of the fifty, the Gulf territory bought from Napoleon in 1803, so the clue names a class and wants an instance.

clue.text: Museum cooled at last, given openings for air

parts.note: the Louvre in Paris is the museum meant

indicators.note: At last marks the end of a run, so it asks for the final letter of the word beside it.

parts.note: the last letter of cooleD

explanation.walkthrough: The Louvre is the museum setters reach for first, and here it is wanted as a string of letters rather than as a place in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: given openings for air → LOUVRED: a louvred door carries angled slats that let a draught through while keeping rain and prying eyes out.

clue.text: Left you to tidy up

parts.note: U is how a text message writes you, and setters adopted it long ago
to neaten is to tidy up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a direction or a departure and is neither — it is food still on the plate when everyone has finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Left → UNEATEN: what is left after a meal is the food nobody touched, so the word means remaining on the plate rather than departed.

clue.text: Missing some gear, rang emporium to order

parts.note: nothing is taken away here — Missing only sets up the shopping story

indicators.note: Some asks for a portion of what follows rather than all of it, so a run of consecutive letters is what you want.

parts.note: the answer runs straight through geARRANGEmporium

explanation.walkthrough: The emporium story is a decoy — nothing is being ordered. The answer spans the join between two words, which is why a comma is such good cover.
explanation.definitionFit: order → ARRANGE: to arrange things is to put them into a chosen order, and the verb also covers fixing up a meeting or scoring music for players.

clue.text: Branch manager may put this up for children's play

definitions.text: Branch manager may put this up for children's play

parts.note: The surface hands you a bank official; the setter means somebody whose branches want managing, which puts you in the garden looking upwards.

parts.words: may put this up for children's play
parts.note: What gets erected among those branches is a small wooden platform with walls, built so the young have somewhere of their own.

explanation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay here: the clue is one picture, and it turns on reading 'branch manager' as a job in a bank before you read it as a job in a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabin built into the limbs of a garden tree is exactly what somebody in charge of branches would raise so youngsters have somewhere to romp.

clue.text: Raise anchor: I contributed

indicators.note: A contribution is something put into a pot, so whatever contributes goes inside the word beside it.

parts.note: the anchor of a news programme is its host
the letter I, taken as itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Anchor' is a television word here rather than a nautical one, which is a neat piece of misdirection in a clue that opens with 'Raise'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raise → HOIST: to hoist is to haul something upward with rope or tackle, the mechanical way of raising a sail, a flag or a load.

clue.text: What one can get from really rich poem

indicators.note: Getting something out of a phrase means lifting the letters straight out of it, unaltered and in the order they already stand.

parts.note: the answer sits across the join in reaLLY RICh

explanation.walkthrough: An adverb and an adjective sit side by side and the answer bridges them, so the trick is to stop reading words and start reading letters.
explanation.definitionFit: poem → LYRIC: a lyric is a short poem of personal feeling, originally one sung to the lyre, so the noun stands perfectly well on its own.

clue.text: Better prepared to fail in the end

indicators.note: Here in does its literal job: whatever comes before it is placed inside whatever comes after.

parts.note: the rear of something is its end
a plan that fails is said to die

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about giving up, and 'the end' is not an instruction about final letters — it is simply a word meaning the back of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Better prepared → READIER: ready means set to go, so its comparative says one party is further along in its preparations than another.

clue.text: The last to leave doomed ship, a drama queen

indicators.note: The last to leave is the one that goes, so the final letter of the word beside it departs and the rest stay.

parts.note: the Titanic is the doomed ship, and its closing C is the one that leaves
the article taken straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drama queen' is an insult on the surface and a job description in the answer: a queen who lives in a play. Shakespeare's fairy monarch is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: drama queen → TITANIA: Titania is the fairy queen of A Midsummer Night's Dream, so the idiom for a histrionic person doubles as queen-in-a-play.

clue.text: Financial claim as tense test drive crashed

indicators.note: A crash leaves the parts of a vehicle strewn about in no particular order, and letters come out of one the same way.

parts.note: the fourteen letters of these three words, resettled

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a road accident and the answer is a legal one. 'Vested' is property-law language: an interest that has already come to you rather than one you might yet acquire.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial claim → VESTED INTEREST: a vested interest is a stake already secured in law, money or property you hold a right to rather than merely hope for.
